claim: A small set of cheap heuristics (find a constant, find a trend, define a ratio or product term, treat defined terms as data and repeat) rediscovers classic product and ratio laws from clean, hand-chosen data. This shows sufficiency of the method, not that scientists worked this way.
agent_test: Give the agent a synthetic law-finding task with clean data and a tolerance-based constancy check in code; compare with the plain model at equal tokens.

claim: Rediscovery of one episode shows one possible path only. A fair test feeds data piecemeal in historical order and must reproduce long-held errors too. Critics add that BACON used cleaned data and variables the programmer chose, unlike the original discoverers.
agent_test: Build a case series in historical order with wrong turns marked; score both right and wrong turns, not only the final law.

claim: Famous laws are recalled, not discovered, by LLMs. Evidence: fast exact fit on Feynman problems (under 20 iterations), lower error and lower perplexity on Feynman than on novel problems, a gap that holds at equal expression size, about half of transformed problems solved after the first iteration, and Kepler/Hubble/Bode data named from context.
agent_test: Never test the schema on named classic laws. Use changed-law, invented-law or variable-renamed versions; flag any exact fit in the first few iterations.

claim: A good numeric fit is not the law. Numeric accuracy can be high while symbolic accuracy is low (material science: Acc0.1 88.28 percent against symbolic 20.24 percent), but symbolic accuracy tracks out-of-domain accuracy, so an extrapolation check is a cheap code proxy for the right form.
agent_test: Require every accepted rule to pass points outside the fitted range; compare fit-only versus extrapolation-checked answers at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A loop that fits and scores candidates in code and feeds real scores back beats one-shot prompting from the model. Data-blind prompting got 2.1 to 7.2 percent symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform; the same backbones inside LLM-SR got about 11 to 32 percent.
agent_test: Run plain model versus generate-test-revise with real tool output on law-finding tasks at equal total tokens.

claim: Let the model write structure and let code fit the numbers. Removing the optimiser (model writes constants) gave Oscillation 2 NMSE of 3.78e-1 in-domain and 3.75e-1 out-of-domain, and removing refinement gave 1.01e-1 and 1.81e-1 (GPT-3.5, one problem). The bilevel LLM plus simulator design also works on an imaginary law.
agent_test: Ablate: model proposes numbers directly versus code fits numbers, same budget.

claim: With memorisation reduced, the best LLM equation system found about a third of the transformed Feynman problems (31.53 percent) and 10 to 28 percent of the synthetic domains. The headline 28.1 percent for LSR-Synth is one cell (LaSR, material science); best per domain was 11.11, 25.30, 9.91, 28.12 (unweighted mean about 18.6).
agent_test: Use tens of percent, not 90, as the expected baseline range; score symbolic accuracy with a code-based equivalence check, not a model judge.

claim: Letting the agent look at the data with code before proposing, and keeping a buffer of top past equations, are the largest ablation effects in an agent loop. Which one dominates depends on the backbone: GPT-OSS-120B lost 27.9 points of Acc0.01 without the analyser; Qwen lost 22.7 without top-k (random sampling instead); GLM lost 11.1 without the experience buffer.
agent_test: Ablate the data-inspection tool and the best-attempts buffer per backbone at equal calls; keep only what wins for that model.

claim: A code interpreter helps weak models and slightly hurts strong ones (GPT-4.1 5.8 to 18.9 percent; Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4 to 63.7; GPT-5 75.9 to 73.3), reportedly because strong models stop exploring early. Cause inferred from traces of two models. Gap search: still no study tests a minimum-hypotheses rule or held-out check against code access at equal tokens; the cause stays inferred from phrase counts in two traces.
agent_test: Test tool access with and without a minimum number of distinct hypotheses before stopping; track exploration rate.

claim: Symbolic accuracy is fragile to small noise and to system complexity. GPT-5-mini lost 12 to 16 percent at noise 0.0001; the hardest NewtonBench setting left only GPT-5 (40.3) and Gemini-2.5-pro (16.7) above 6 percent. AI Feynman 1.0 is brittle with noise in SRBench and v2 gained 1 to 3 orders of noise robustness.
agent_test: Add a small-noise rerun of the final answer; an answer that flips is rejected.

claim: Author-reported headlines shrink under independent testing: AI Feynman 100 of 100 on its own set became 53 percent exact recovery noise-free in SRBench and fell behind other methods above noise 0.01. The SRBench figures were not re-opened by the cross-checker. Gap search: on the 129 LSR-Synth tasks a semantics-blind fixed library (77.7 percent Acc0.01) beat every earlier LLM-system report (best 63.6), so published LLM-system headlines also need a no-LLM bank arm.
agent_test: Run our own held-out comparison rather than quoting authors; use repeated seeds.

claim: Meaningful names and domain context carry real signal for LLM equation discovery (variable names removed: biggest LaSR slowdown; prior removed: big LLM-SR loss; PhysGym top models 66 to 31 percent as priors fall). The effect is not monotone per problem, so context can also mislead.
agent_test: Run each task with names and context on and stripped; use the difference to separate recall from inference.

claim: Adding an LLM-built concept library to genetic search raised exact Feynman solves from 59 to 72 of 100, but PySR given 10 hours per equation reaches about 62, the abstract says 66, and a memorisation-controlled benchmark found LaSR weak (5.4 to 12.6 percent symbolic on LSR-Transform, 0 to 28 percent on synthetic domains).
agent_test: Compare a small code-gated lesson store against no store at equal tokens on changed-law tasks, not on Feynman.

claim: Reasoning-trained models dominate: NewtonBench overall symbolic accuracy GPT-5 75.9, Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4, o4-mini 47.8 versus 5.1 to 8.9 for GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini and DeepSeek-V3, at about 19k tokens per task for GPT-5. A scaffold must be judged against a reasoning-model baseline.
agent_test: Always include the strongest reasoning baseline at equal tokens before claiming a scaffold gain.

claim: Whole-loop discovery by LLM agents is far below humans and below 50 percent on every benchmark that tests it: DiscoveryWorld completion 0.08 to 0.38 versus humans 0.66; DiscoveryBench best 25 percent; FIRE-Bench best F1 46.7.
agent_test: Use DiscoveryWorld-style invented worlds as the whole-loop test, since they remove memory.

claim: Agent errors sit in research planning, control design and the conclusions drawn, not in coding. In FIRE-Bench contradictory plus unrelated claims were 76.4 to 95.0 percent of false positives and alternative explanations only 4.5 to 10.9 percent; controls were the weakest part. DiscoveryBench domains with near-zero success (biology 0) show where search does not help. Gap search: the FIRE-Bench stage shares were seen only in a chart; the claim that a code claim-versus-output check would close the gap is untested.
agent_test: Add a code check that each stated conclusion appears in the executed output; measure the drop in contradicted claims.

claim: Run-to-run variance is large, so one run proves little: FIRE-Bench median coefficient of variation 0.37 for Claude Code and above 0.6 for OpenHands; SR-Scientist and NewtonBench report averages of 3 to 4 runs with wide intervals.
agent_test: Use at least 3 to 5 seeds per arm and report intervals.

claim: Pick winners among candidates that fit equally well with a derivation, theory or constraint check, or a complexity trade-off computed in code: AI Descartes ranks fits by reasoning error against axioms; AI Feynman 2.0 keeps a Pareto frontier of accuracy against description length; constraints in the prompt raised meaningful equations but did not beat PySR on complex targets. Gap search: in SciLaws-Bench the best candidate in a run beat the submitted law by 0.14 (GPT-5.4-mini) versus 0.03 to 0.04 (GPT-6, Opus 5.5), and self-selection kept under 2 of the 4.5 to 5.3 points an oracle gains; fit and validity agree on only 53.6 percent of pairs.
agent_test: Break ties with a code-computed derivation or MDL score, not the model's opinion; test against pure-fit selection.

claim: Narrowing by structure before fitting works: dimensional analysis, symmetry and separability (AI Feynman), units (ABACUS), physics tools before PySINDy/PySR (KeplerAgent: 42.34 percent with 3 attempts). It helps most on real physics and less on arbitrary compositions (66.7 versus 48.9 percent against Eureqa on non-physical functions). Gap search: the lift is not general. KeplerAgent (GPT-4o-mini) went from 30/10 (PySR) to 75/45 percent symbolic accuracy on clean/noisy ODE systems, but on transformed-Feynman LSR-Transform one run (35.1) stayed under plain PySR (37.8) and only best-of-3 (42.3) passed it. Units and separability probes were not tested with an LLM agent.
agent_test: Add a structure-probe step (units, symmetry, separability) run in code before generation; measure solve rate versus no probe.

claim: Order and incrementality matter for cost and for reuse: BACON.3 reached the same law in any data order but cost differed (Ohm 4593 productions); STAHL needs historical order; AI-Newton builds simple concepts (mass) before hard ones (force) and reuses them across experiments.
agent_test: Compare shuffled versus staged order of sub-problems on a multi-step task at equal tokens; check the same final answer.

claim: Without a code-side redundancy check the term search explodes: BACON.3 defined 31 terms and rejected 84 redundant ones for Ohm's law, versus 1 to 12 for the other laws.
agent_test: Add a code duplicate and equivalence filter on candidates; count tokens saved.

claim: Laws need scope conditions: ABACUS learns separate equations for data subsets with stated conditions; BACON.1 never rejects a hypothesis once formed and cannot do conditional laws. Sums and differences stay much harder than products and ratios.
agent_test: When a rule fails on a subset, test splitting it by condition instead of replacing it; compare scope-keeping revisions with overwriting ones.

claim: Decomposing hypothesis generation into retrieve inspiration, compose, then rank works for held-out chemistry hypotheses (inspiration hit ratio 83.7 percent for GPT-4o at top 4 percent kept, 43.5 for Llama-8B), but model self-ranking of hypotheses tracks match weakly (rank ratio 0.411 to 0.521).
agent_test: Test retrieve-then-combine against free generation with code-run evaluation, not model ranking.

claim: Disguised or counterfactual tests are feasible but give mixed contamination signals: renaming variables stopped GPT-5 recalling Kepler's third law (anecdote), changed-law and invented-law designs lower scores sharply, yet FIRE-Bench found no clear pre/post-cutoff difference in ML-paper rediscovery. Gap search: renaming gave a graded effect (Acc0.01 49.8 vs 41.1 with names hidden); a cold-recall tier audit predicts published-form recovery (92 vs 61 percent) but not full new-structure recovery (flat 12 to 13 percent); FIRE-Bench cutoff cells hold 1 to 8 tasks each. So the controls measure different things; none has been shown to predict out-of-distribution scores best.
agent_test: Run each task in original, renamed and altered-law versions; compare pass rate across versions.

claim: An agent can repeat failures: in a KeplerAgent appendix case the agent stayed at 15.6 percent MAPE on noisy data without learning from earlier attempts; the experience-buffer ablations in SR-Scientist point to the same weakness.
agent_test: Check whether a failed-attempt store that keeps the failing output cuts repeated mistakes.

claim: Humans rediscovering a law are a minority: in a laboratory replication 4 of 14 subjects found Kepler's law (about 29 percent). Seen only in a search summary. Gap search: Qin and Simon (1990) and Klahr and Simon (1999) were still not readable (paywall, 403); this figure stays unverified.
agent_test: Use human pass rates as the bar when scoring rediscovery of the same data.

claim: Human bar from the founding study: in Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Study 1, 19 of 20 adults found a hidden BigTrak REPEAT rule within 45 minutes (mean 19.8 min, 18.2 programs), and no one started with the right rule. Seen in the full paper.
agent_test: Run the same toy-device task for an LLM agent and compare solve rate, programs to solution and share of experiments with no stated hypothesis.

claim: Dual-space reading holds in the human data: 13 of 20 people could not generate the right frame from memory and found it only through an experiment in a particular region of the experiment space (24.5 min, 18.3 experiments); the 7 who generated it from memory took 11.4 min and 9.3 experiments. People kept a disconfirmed hypothesis in 76 of 136 disconfirming outcomes and dropped a confirmed one in 21 of 84. Strategy is confounded with programming experience (7 of 7 vs 1 of 13). In Study 2 (N=10) listing hypotheses first put the right rule on the list for 5 of 10 and everyone then solved it in 6.2 min.
schema_part: O-operators for hypothesis listing and discriminating experiments; G for switching after a miss
agent_test: Code LLM traces by which space produced the escape from a wrong frame; add a forced switch after a disconfirming result and compare retention rate with the human 56 percent.

claim: A semantics-blind fixed library of generic terms with the same fitter solved most LLM-SRBench synthetic tasks (Acc0.01 77.7 percent, strict ID+OOD 39.5) and beat LLM-proposed terms alone (49.8; 13.8). Adding LLM terms changed nothing with the full library (77.3 to 77.7) and helped only when the library was cut to polynomials (27.5 to 58.1). Names and context still carry signal (49.8 vs 41.1 when hidden).
agent_test: For any scaffold test on equation tasks, include a no-LLM term bank at the same fitting budget and report the paired gain.

claim: Selection, not generation, is the weak step on current models: the best candidate an agent evaluated beat its submitted law by 0.14 (a weak model) and 0.03 to 0.04 (GPT-6, Opus 5.5), and model self-selection kept under 2 of the 4.5 to 5.3 points an oracle would gain. A held-out score check was not tried, so it is a lead, not a result.
agent_test: Add a code step that scores every candidate on held-out points and submits the best; compare with self-selection at equal tokens.

claim: Division of labour: with one backbone and equal compute, letting the model plan the search while code enumerates and numeric gates retain candidates gave ACC0.1 0.958 at 91k tokens, versus 0.892 and 450k tokens when the model wrote equations and 0.665 to 0.892 at 2.2M to 2.8M tokens for full LLM systems. Plain PySR was 0.922. Model-written equations collapsed on atypical formulas; model-judged retention failed on a near-tie.
schema_part: fit and retain in code; model proposes structure
agent_test: Compare a reasoning model with code access against the controller split at equal tokens on altered-law tasks.

claim: Recall of the published formula predicts recovery of the published form (92 percent for always-recalled tasks, 61 percent for never-recalled) but not recovery of a new structural variant (12 to 13 percent in every tier; best model 42 percent overall). Best current model still gets only 72 percent structure score on the invented-variant setting.
agent_test: Score published-form recovery and new-structure recovery separately; do not pool them.

claim: No LLM study was found that (a) codes agent traces as hypothesis-space versus experiment-space search, (b) feeds a model a historical case series in order and checks for the historical wrong turns, or (c) compares scope-tagged revision with overwrite on conditional laws. The search was cut short by rate limits and the claim is weak.
schema_part: design of the project's own rediscovery test
agent_test: Build the three tests ourselves: trace coding with the Klahr and Dunbar categories; ordered case series; conditional-law tasks with a scope-split arm.
